analysis.one_liner: Expands voting access, tightens campaign money disclosure, and sets ethics rules for all three branches of government.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill itself: a June 2021 procedural vote to begin debate failed 50-50, with all 50 Republicans opposed, and a second attempt's cloture motion was withdrawn in September.
analysis.plain_summary: The For the People Act would make registration and voting easier — automatic, online, and same-day registration, plus guaranteed early and mail voting — and set limits on removing voters from the rolls. It would take congressional district drawing away from partisan legislators and give it to independent state commissions, require disclosure of big-money campaign spending, curb foreign money, and offer public matching funds to candidates who raise small donations. It would also add ethics rules: a code of conduct for federal judges including Supreme Court justices, a ban on House members serving on for-profit corporate boards, and 10 years of tax-return disclosure for presidents and vice presidents.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters — especially low-income, disabled, young, and minority voters who face the largest barriers to registration and voting — gain easier registration, more days and ways to vote, and protections against voter purges and polling place interference. Candidates who rely on small donors gain public matching funds; the public gains disclosure of who is paying for political ads and lobbying, independent-drawn congressional districts, judges bound by an ethics code, and presidents required to disclose their tax returns.

how_it_helps.text: Requires states to offer automatic, online, and same-day voter registration, and expands vote-by-mail and early voting [S2]
Limits removing voters from the rolls and bans deceptive practices, voter caging, and intimidation at the polls [S2]
Requires states to draw congressional districts with independent redistricting commissions instead of partisan legislators, and bans mid-decade redistricting [S2]
Requires disclosure of campaign-related fundraising and spending, adds disclaimers to online political ads, and expands the ban on campaign spending by foreign nationals [S2]
Creates an alternative public campaign-funding system so candidates can run on small donations rather than large checks [S2]

Sets a code of conduct for federal judges including Supreme Court justices, bars House members from for-profit corporate boards, tightens conflict-of-interest rules for federal employees and the White House, and requires presidents and vice presidents to disclose 10 years of tax returns [S2]
Funds states to secure election systems, requires voter-verifiable paper ballots and post-election audits, and shares intelligence threat information with state election officials [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Large political donors and super PACs would lose secrecy over their spending; lobbying firms, foreign agents, and online ad platforms would face new disclosure and registration rules; state legislatures would lose the power to draw congressional districts to their own party's advantage; campaigns would bear compliance costs; and the small-donor matching-fund program would be paid for with federal money. Incumbent officeholders would face new ethics, recusal, and financial-disclosure rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big donors, platforms, lobbying firms, incumbents

drawbacks.text: The bill would override state election procedures with federal standards, replacing how states currently run registration, voting, and congressional redistricting — a significant shift of power from states to Washington that courts would have tested [S3]
The small-donor matching-fund program for Senate and presidential candidates would be financed with public money, a cost taxpayers would bear directly [S2]

Automatic registration would transfer data from many government agencies to election officials unless individuals affirmatively decline, raising accuracy and privacy questions that the bill addresses through opt-out and security provisions but does not eliminate [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core voting-access provisions extend practices many states already run — online registration, early voting, mail ballots — to every state, at modest cost offset by federal grants. The heaviest costs fall not on ordinary people but on the interests the bill regulates: donors seeking anonymity, lobbying firms, and legislators who draw their own districts. The serious tradeoffs are the federalism question of Congress superseding state election administration and the ongoing taxpayer cost of public campaign financing; both are real, but they do not outweigh the access, disclosure, and ethics gains for the public.

outcome.mechanism: Twice the bill came to the Senate floor only to fail the chamber's rule requiring 60 votes to start debate; after the second attempt's cloture motion was withdrawn, it never received an up-or-down vote and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 16, 2021, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar (Calendar No. 77) [S5]
On June 22, 2021, cloture on the motion to proceed failed 50-50 — short of the 60 votes needed to begin debate [S6]
All 48 Senate Democrats and both independents voted to proceed; all 50 Republicans voted no [S6]
A second motion to proceed and cloture motion were filed on August 11, 2021; the cloture motion was withdrawn by unanimous consent on September 15, 2021 [S5]
The bill never received a vote on its merits, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 without it becoming law [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The interests the bill would have regulated are better off because it died: large donors and super PACs keep their spending undisclosed, lobbying firms and foreign agents avoid tighter registration and enforcement, state legislators keep drawing congressional maps to their party's advantage, and incumbent officeholders avoid a Supreme Court ethics code, tighter conflict-of-interest rules, and presidential tax-return disclosure. No voter gained any of the bill's access protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big donors, super PACs, and incumbents

sides.party_line_note: On the June 22, 2021 cloture vote, all 48 Democrats and both independents voted to proceed and all 50 Republicans voted no — a fully partisan split, with the bill short of the 60 votes the Senate requires to start debate.

industries.industry: Large political donors and super PACs
industries.note: The bill would have required disclosure of large political fundraising and spending, expanded the ban on foreign money, and offered public matching funds so campaigns need fewer giant checks. Its defeat preserves the current system where a small pool of very large donors funds elections largely out of public view.

industries.industry: Incumbent officeholders and state legislative mapmakers
industries.note: The bill would have moved congressional redistricting to independent commissions, banned mid-decade gerrymandering, imposed an ethics code on federal judges including Supreme Court justices, barred House members from for-profit boards, and required presidents to disclose 10 years of tax returns. Blocking it keeps district-drawing power with the legislators who benefit from the maps and keeps existing ethics gaps open.

The bill would have expanded who counts as a lobbyist under disclosure law, created a Justice Department unit to enforce foreign-agent registration, and banned foreign lobbying. Its defeat leaves current disclosure thresholds and enforcement in place.

The Honest Ads provisions would have required online platforms to identify the sponsors of political ads, keep those notices when ads are shared, and maintain records of political ad purchases. The defeat avoids those compliance obligations, at the cost of keeping online political ad money harder to trace.

The bill would have required US-manufactured machines, voter-verifiable paper ballots, and new cybersecurity standards — new compliance costs — while federal grant programs would pay states to upgrade to compliant systems, creating a revenue stream.
